title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: In §XI (previous page) Euler sets up an element of a plane filament with three unknowns: tangential tension T, normal (shear) force V, and a lever arm v. The bending moment is written as the product M = V·v. Balancing tangential forces, normal forces and moments about the point m under distributed loads p (tangential) and q (normal) per unit length gives three equations: (I) dT + V dΦ = p ds; (II) dV − T dΦ = q ds; (III) d(Vv) = V ds, i.e. dM/ds = V. Here Φ is the tangent angle, so dΦ/ds = κ is the curvature. §XII says the general solution will now be specialised to two principal cases.

Case 1 (this page), perfectly flexible string. A string cannot carry shear or bending moment, so V = 0. Equation III then holds trivially. The other two reduce to the classical intrinsic equilibrium equations of a loaded string: dT/ds = p and −Tκ = q. Integrating I gives T = ∫p ds (an integration constant, i.e. a reference tension, is implicit). Equation II gives T = −q ds/dΦ. Eliminating T yields dΦ = −q ds / ∫p ds. This is an intrinsic (Cesàro-type) equation κ(s) = −q(s)/∫p ds for the funicular curve. It contains only data, provided p and q are prescribed as functions of arc length. Examples are promised later in the memoir.

Case 2 (§XIII, begun here), uniformly elastic rod that is straight in its natural state. Euler adopts the Jakob Bernoulli–Euler bending law: bending moment = A·κ = A dΦ/ds, with constant stiffness A. Writing the moment as Vv gives the constitutive equation Vv = A dΦ/ds, to be combined with I–III.

On the next page this leads (ds constant) to:
- V = A κ';
- T = ∫p ds − Aκ²/2;
- V = (Aκ'' − q)/κ from II.
Equating the two expressions for T gives 2Aκ'' + Aκ³ = 2κ∫p ds + 2q. This is the standard intrinsic fourth-order (in position) equation of the planar elastica under arbitrary distributed tangential and normal loads. I checked the algebra and it is correct.
errors: No algebraic error on this page. The integration constant in T = ∫p ds is left implicit; it is absorbed in the indefinite integral, but in applications it is the physically essential end tension.

Conceptual awkwardness, not an outright error: representing the bending moment as M = V·v (shear force times a lever arm) breaks down for pure bending. There V = 0 while M = Aκ ≠ 0, so v must be infinite. Correspondingly, Euler's later formula v = ds dΦ/ddΦ is infinite for constant curvature. The independent moment variable M = Aκ would be cleaner; Euler's equations are formally right where v is finite.
Distributed couples are not admitted in the moment balance. This is consistent with the loading assumed, so it is not an error, only a restriction.

ideas.what: Intrinsic equilibrium equations of a perfectly flexible string under tangential and normal distributed loads: dT/ds = p, −Tκ = q
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (tangential/normal) equations of the funicular / loaded string
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob and Johann Bernoulli, Hermann (c. 1690s–1716); Euler in various earlier works
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier treatments of strings and catenaries, and this memoir E410 (Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 15); analysed by Truesdell, Opera omnia II 11/2

ideas.what: Elimination of tension giving dΦ = −q ds / ∫p ds, an intrinsic equation of the equilibrium curve purely in terms of given loads
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (curvature vs. arc-length) equation of the funicular curve
ideas.where_published: E410 explicitly; similar forms likely in earlier Euler string papers (unsure of exact location)

ideas.what: Shear force V as an independent unknown, with balance of moments d(Vv) = V ds (shear = derivative of moment) added to force balance
ideas.modern_name: Balance of linear and angular momentum for rods; the shear–moment relation dM/ds = V
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, precisely in this memoir E410 (1771), as emphasised by Truesdell
ideas.where_published: E410 itself; discussed at length in Truesdell, 'Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788' (Opera omnia II 11/2, 1960)

ideas.what: Constitutive law: bending moment proportional to curvature, M = A dΦ/ds, for a naturally straight, uniformly elastic rod
ideas.modern_name: Bernoulli–Euler bending law (flexural rigidity A = EI)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli (1694), Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1744 elastica appendix to the Methodus inveniendi)
ideas.where_published: E65 (Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I, 1744) and later Euler papers; E410

deep.surprise_reason: The page specialises Euler's general rod equations to the flexible string (classical intrinsic equations) and begins the uniformly elastic case with the Bernoulli–Euler law. E410's role in introducing shear force and moment balance is well documented by Truesdell. Nothing here appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially; only minor orthographic variants (e.g. 'obseruasse' is hyphenated 'obser-vasse' across lines in the print).
